Dung
dung
n.
Old English dung, manure. Webster 1828: the excrement of animals. The Authorized Version uses the word without flinching, and its translators chose it deliberately in Philippians 3:8, where the Greek is a coarse term for refuse. Scripture’s realism about filth is part of its doctrine of holiness.

Biblical Definition

Dung is Scripture’s blunt word for what must be carried outside, and it is used with theological precision. In the sin offering, the parts that bore the guilt were removed from the camp entire: the bullock for the sin offering, and the goat for the sin offering, whose blood was brought in to make atonement in the holy place, shall one carry forth without the camp; and they shall burn in the fire their skins, and their flesh, and their dung (Leviticus 16:27). Nothing of the sin-bearer stayed inside. Hebrews reads that ritual as pointing to Christ suffering without the gate. The prophets use the word for the shame of judgment — the unburied dead lie for dung upon the face of the earth (Jeremiah 8:2) — and Malachi turns it on corrupt priests with shocking directness: I will spread dung upon your faces, even the dung of your solemn feasts (Malachi 2:3). The offerings they profaned become the filth that marks them. Then Paul, listing his pedigree, circumcision, tribe, blamelessness under law, weighs it all and reaches for the same category: I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord... and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ (Philippians 3:8). Not worthless things — his best things, and he calls them refuse beside Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DUNG as the excrement of animals; and as a verb, to manure with dung, or to enrich land. Webster also records the compound uses the Authorized Version knows: dunghill, dung-gate, dung-port.

expand to see more

DUNG, n. — The excrement of animals. DUNG, v.t. — To manure with dung; to enrich land by spreading dung upon it.

Webster notes the agricultural use, and Scripture assumes it too — the fig tree in the parable is dunged in the hope of fruit. But the Authorized Version’s theological uses are all removal, not enrichment: dung goes outside the camp, outside the gate, off the altar. Where the word appears in the sanctuary it marks what may not remain.

Key Scripture

Philippians 3:8 — "Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,"

Leviticus 16:27 — "And the bullock for the sin offering, and the goat for the sin offering, whose blood was brought in to make atonement in the holy place, shall one carry forth without the camp; and they shall burn in the fire their skins, and their flesh, and their dung."

Malachi 2:3 — "Behold, I will corrupt your seed, and spread dung upon your faces, even the dung of your solemn feasts; and one shall take you away with it."

Jeremiah 8:2 — "And they shall spread them before the sun, and the moon, and all the host of heaven, whom they have loved, and whom they have served, and after whom they have walked, and whom they have sought, and whom they have worshipped: they shall not be gathered, nor be buried; they shall be for dung upon the face of the earth."

Modern Corruption

Dung is corrupted mainly by softening — modern renderings and modern preaching blunt Philippians 3:8 into rubbish or garbage, which loses Paul’s deliberate coarseness and, with it, the violence of the comparison he is making.

expand to see more

Paul chose a crude word on purpose, and the Authorized Version translated it honestly. The refinement of dung into rubbish is not merely a matter of taste; it changes the argument. Rubbish is neutral waste, discarded without feeling. Dung is offensive, and it is offensive precisely because it was once food. Paul’s list is not of sins he abandoned but of genuine advantages — covenant circumcision, the tribe of Benjamin, the law’s blamelessness — the very things a devout man would count as gain. He says that beside Christ these become excrement. The doctrine of justification requires that violence. Self-righteousness is not merely insufficient; it is filthy, and Isaiah had already said as much of our righteousnesses. A translation that spares the reader spares him the doctrine.

The second misuse runs opposite, and it appears wherever Philippians 3 is read as contempt for God’s good gifts. Paul is not despising circumcision, the law, or his people; he defends all three elsewhere at length. The word is comparative and situational: these things are dung that I may win Christ. Held as gain over against Christ, a lawful advantage becomes refuse; held under Christ, it is honoured. Leviticus 16:27 makes the same point ritually — what is carried outside the camp is not garbage swept from the floor but the sin offering itself, the holiest animal in the service, bearing what cannot be allowed to remain. The category is not worthless. It is must go outside.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Several Hebrew nouns for refuse and animal waste lie behind the Old Testament’s dung, and one blunt Greek noun behind Paul’s. The consistent thread is not disgust for its own sake but exclusion — what belongs outside the camp.

expand to see more

Greek skubalon — refuse, offal, dung; what is thrown to the dogs (Philippians 3:8). A deliberately coarse word, and the Authorized Version renders it plainly. Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.

Hebrew gelēl (H1557) — dung, a dung ball; the root also underlies the contemptuous word the prophets use for idols.

Hebrew peresh — the offal of a sacrificial animal, carried outside the camp with the skin and flesh (Leviticus 16:27). Untagged in this lexicon.

That the prophets’ word for idols shares a root with dung is not accidental; Ezekiel in particular uses it as a standing insult to what Israel worshipped.

Usage

"The sin offering was burnt without the camp, skin, flesh and dung together (Leviticus 16:27) — the sin-bearer goes entirely outside."

"Malachi threatens corrupt priests with the dung of your solemn feasts (Malachi 2:3): their own offerings become their disgrace."

"Paul counts his best credentials but dung, that I may win Christ (Philippians 3:8). The word is coarse on purpose."
